title: Diljit's Main Vaapas Aaunga Showed a Pakistan Without Villains. The Internet Cried 'Anti-National.' A.R. Rahman Just Laughed.
excerpt: Imtiaz Ali's softest film in years is quietly climbing past 26 crore worldwide — and its crime, apparently, is showing a Pakistan without villains.
body:
It opens not with a bang but with a breath. **Diljit Dosanjh**, all warmth and weathered charm, moving through a world that **Imtiaz Ali** has built the way he always does — drenched in longing, lit like a half-remembered dream. There are no terrorists lurking in shadows here, no secret agents with cold eyes. There is only love, and distance, and the ache of a man trying to find his way back to someone. And somehow, in 2026, that was enough to set the internet on fire.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8</youtube>

**Main Vaapas Aaunga** is the kind of film that shouldn't be controversial. A partition-era romance from the director who gave us *Jab We Met* and *Rockstar*, scored by **A.R. Rahman**, starring Diljit at his most disarming alongside **Naseeruddin Shah**, **Sharvari**, and **Vedang Raina**. It is gentle. It is unhurried. It believes, almost stubbornly, in the better parts of people. And that belief is precisely what got it labelled.

A satirical post made the rounds last week, jeering: "Anti-national? Movie dares to show Pakistan without terrorists and secret agents." It was a joke about the joke — a wink at how reflexively certain corners of the discourse now reach for the word the moment a film declines to draw the usual villains. Rahman, never one to wade into shouting matches, reposted it with a single laughing emoji. No statement, no thread, no wounded press note. Just a man who has scored more cross-border longing than anyone alive, declining to dignify the noise.

> "Tere Paas Main is the beating heart of Main Vaapas Aaunga. As we go through the ups and downs of life, each one of us has a happy place in our hearts that we go to and feel better instantly." — Imtiaz Ali

That happy place arrived in song form this week. On what the makers swear was "popular demand," Imtiaz released **Tere Paas Main**, a Rahman composition so sparse it almost dares you to lean in. Written by **Irshad Kamil** and sung by **Deepali Sahay**, it is the rare film track that trusts silence — a sarod here, a Prague string section there, a flute that seems to exhale rather than play. "We had no intention of bringing out this cut now," Imtiaz admitted. "We are doing so only because of popular demand by the audience. Long live cinema." It is a flex disguised as humility, and it works.

What makes the film land for the diaspora isn't the controversy — it's the proposition underneath it. For NRIs who carry partition in their family histories the way some carry heirlooms, a story that looks across the border and sees people rather than props is not provocation. It is recognition. Diljit, who has spent the last two years turning Punjabi identity into a global export, is exactly the face for it: a man whose very stardom is built on softness, on melody, on the refusal to perform the rage that's expected of him.

The numbers say audiences agree. The film opened June 12 and has built quietly rather than exploded — the way Imtiaz films tend to. By day eight it had crossed **26 crore worldwide gross**, with overseas markets contributing a healthy 9.25 crore. That overseas figure is the tell: this is a film finding its people in the very diaspora it's about, in cinema halls in Edison and Brampton and Southall where partition isn't history but inheritance. At its current pace it's tracking to cross 30 crore — modest by tentpole standards, but exactly the kind of slow, word-of-mouth burn that gentle films live or die by.

Diljit is on a tear besides. The same week, A.R. Rahman dropped *Tere Paas Main*'s companion piece for the actor's other project, and Los Angeles handed Dosanjh his own civic day on the city calendar. The boy from Dosanjh Kalan is, somehow, everywhere — and choosing, again and again, projects that lead with tenderness rather than fury.

**Where to watch:** *Main Vaapas Aaunga* is in cinemas worldwide now, including most major US, UK, and Canada markets through the usual NRI-friendly chains. No streaming date has been announced yet — though given Imtiaz's catalogue tends to find a long second life online, expect an OTT landing later this year. For now, this is one to catch on the big screen, while the strings still fill the room.
